parts.note: a steady easy pace, read as a pace that nudges or jogs the memory

explanation.surface: A walking rhythm that seems to aid recall.
explanation.walkthrough: To jog the memory is to prompt it, and a trot is a pace, so the name of this plodding gait seems built to help you remember.
explanation.definitionFit: A jogtrot is a slow, steady, monotonous running pace.

parts.note: a jumbo is a large jet airliner
Uncle Sam personifies the United States

explanation.surface: An elephant's keeper cast off a ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumbo' looks like an elephant; it is the airliner.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods cast off a ship to lighten it, which are said to be jettisoned.

definitions.note: an adjective standing for a tasty dish

indicators.note: dealing the cards again mixes them up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Dealing the cards again in Slough proves delightful.
explanation.walkthrough: 're-deal' rearranges A SLOUGH; in bridge a goulash is in fact a re-deal of unshuffled hands, a neat extra layer. Slough is a town west of London.
explanation.definitionFit: A rich Hungarian meat stew seasoned with paprika, a flavourful dish.

clue.text: In which to live luxuriously and flush?

definitions.text: In which to live luxuriously and flush?

parts.words: In which to live luxuriously and flush?
parts.note: to live in clover is to live in luxury, and to flush is to turn red

explanation.surface: A question about where to live well and be rich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flush' looks like being well off; it is blushing red, and living 'in clover' is the idiom for luxury.
explanation.definitionFit: A common field plant with reddish-purple flower heads, grown for fodder.

parts.note: treble means threefold
choirs are bodies of voices

explanation.surface: A music festival for boy sopranos.
explanation.walkthrough: 'treble voices' looks like high boys' voices; it is three choirs. The festival is an annual meeting of the cathedral choirs of Gloucester, Hereford and Worcester in western England.
explanation.definitionFit: The long-running English music festival rotating between three cathedral cities.

parts.note: a husker strips the outer leaves from ears of maize, and his pipe is made from the woody core of one

explanation.surface: What a farmhand puffs on.
explanation.walkthrough: The American farm pipe is carved from the core of an ear of maize, the very thing a husker handles all day.
explanation.definitionFit: A tobacco pipe with a bowl made from the dried core of a maize ear, typical of American farmers.

clue.text: Return of the swallow, Mrs. Moo

definitions.text: Return of the swallow, Mrs. Moo

parts.words: Return of the swallow, Mrs. Moo
parts.note: a cow brings back food it has swallowed to chew it again

explanation.surface: Announcing to a cow that the swallow bird has come back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swallow' looks like the migrating bird; it is a mouthful swallowed and brought back up by 'Mrs Moo', a cow.
explanation.definitionFit: Partly digested food that a ruminant brings back from its stomach to chew again.

clue.text: Novel in the vernacular that conquered France

definitions.text: Novel in the vernacular that conquered France

parts.words: Novel in the vernacular that conquered France
parts.note: the French word for a novel, and the people of the empire that conquered Gaul

explanation.surface: A book in the everyday tongue that took France by storm.
explanation.walkthrough: The French for 'novel' is the same word that names the people who conquered Gaul, now France.
explanation.definitionFit: In French a novel is so called, and Julius Caesar's legions from Italy conquered Gaul.

parts.note: a London suburb's name with its letters rearranged gives a stock shepherd's name from pastoral poetry

explanation.surface: A rural version of a suburban London town.
explanation.walkthrough: Croydon is a built-up London suburb; shuffle its letters and you get the shepherd of Virgil's eclogues, the most pastoral of names.
explanation.definitionFit: A conventional shepherd's name in pastoral poetry, from Virgil's Eclogues.

definitions.meaning: a lantern with a thick bulging lens
a large round striped peppermint candy

explanation.definitionFit: The name is shared by an old lantern with a convex glass and a hard round peppermint sweet.

parts.note: applause for a showy performance, read as a storm whose claps follow its flashes of lightning

explanation.surface: An audience applauding a showy performance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clapped' looks like applause; it is the clap of a storm, and the 'flashy show' is lightning.
explanation.definitionFit: A storm's claps are its loud rumbles, and a delighted audience that roared its applause is said to have done the same.

parts.note: in A Midsummer Night's Dream the tinker Snout plays Wall in the mechanicals' play

explanation.surface: A role in a play for a character with a comic name.
explanation.walkthrough: Snout, in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, plays Wall; a painting on a wall is the 'artistic' sense of the word meaning 'of a wall'.
explanation.definitionFit: A wall painting; the word comes from Latin murus, a wall, which was Snout's role.

clue.text: Help! St. Teresa's town in ruins

indicators.note: a town in ruins is broken up, so the name's letters are rearranged

parts.note: St Teresa of Avila is named after her Spanish home town

explanation.surface: A cry for aid for a saint's ruined birthplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in ruins' rearranges AVILA, the Spanish town of St Teresa, into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To be of avail is to be of use or assistance, so the noun means benefit or aid.

clue.text: Well Greek chaps, a fatal date in Rome for good-natured ladies

parts.note: eu is the Greek word for well, as in euphoria
chaps are men
the Ides of March, when Julius Caesar was killed in Rome

explanation.surface: Greek men and a deadly Roman day somehow linked to kindly women.
explanation.walkthrough: The Furies of Greek myth were called by this flattering name, 'the kindly ones', to avoid angering them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek name means the gracious or kindly ones, a euphemism for the avenging Furies.

indicators.note: the letters of the words are taken in such a form as the answer needs, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Royal claimants ruling over kingdoms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In such' signals that REALMS REIGN is to be rearranged. 'Pretenders' suggests rival claimants to a throne; it means people who fake illness to avoid work.
explanation.definitionFit: Shirkers who feign sickness to dodge duty are pretending to be ill.

parts.note: a pub game played by pushing coins along a board, named for a coin that has been withdrawn

explanation.surface: A pastime that has fallen out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: The pub game's name includes a British coin that stopped being legal tender in 1969, so the coin is 'no longer given currency' even if the game survives.
explanation.definitionFit: A British pub game in which coins are pushed with the hand up a marked board.

clue.text: Something that was simmering in an author's brain ?

definitions.text: Something that was simmering in an author's brain ?

parts.words: Something that was simmering in an author's brain ?
parts.note: a cooking pot on the boil, standing for hack work written just to earn a living

explanation.surface: An idea bubbling away in a writer's mind.
explanation.walkthrough: A hack writes to 'keep the pot boiling', that is to pay for food, so a cheap novel was on the simmer in the writer's head.
explanation.definitionFit: A book written merely to make money, keeping the cooking pot on the fire.

parts.note: astra is Latin for stars, as in the motto per ardua ad astra
a gal is a girl or lass

explanation.surface: A model of the stars made by a girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moulding' looks like shaping; it is the architectural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A small convex moulding of semicircular section round a column.

parts.note: an independent nation, read as the condition of a British gold coin

explanation.surface: A nation whose money is backed by gold.
explanation.walkthrough: A sovereign is a British gold coin, so a country standing on gold is a sovereign's state.
explanation.definitionFit: An independent nation governing itself with full authority.

parts.note: the song says old soldiers never die, they simply fade away

explanation.surface: An old soldier who is past his prime but undying.
explanation.walkthrough: The barrack-room song 'Old soldiers never die, they simply fade away' makes the old campaigner both immortal and faded.
explanation.definitionFit: An old soldier with long service, one who in the song never dies.

clue.text: Storm that's rent much work of Shakespeare's

parts.note: rent is the past participle of rend, torn
Much Ado About Nothing, by Shakespeare; ado means fuss

explanation.surface: A tempest that tore through a Shakespeare play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like payment; it is the past of rend. 'Much' ties to Shakespeare's comedy Much Ado About Nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent rotating windstorm, a whirlwind.

parts.note: the church season before Christmas, whose name means arrival

explanation.surface: The next season ahead.
explanation.walkthrough: Not just 'the next season': the name of the period before Christmas means 'coming' in Latin.
explanation.definitionFit: The four weeks before Christmas, from Latin adventus, arrival.

clue.text: The nose of my Lady Disdain?

definitions.text: The nose of my Lady Disdain?

parts.words: The nose of my Lady Disdain?
parts.note: Benedick calls Beatrice 'my dear Lady Disdain' in Much Ado About Nothing; a disdainful person turns up her nose

explanation.surface: A question about the profile of a scornful heroine.
explanation.walkthrough: A nose turned up at the tip is the classic sign of disdain, so Shakespeare's 'Lady Disdain' must have one.
explanation.definitionFit: Said of a nose, turned up at the tip, the expression of someone looking down on others.

clue.text: What's the hue and cry of Celts about?

parts.note: och is a Scottish and Irish exclamation
re means about, concerning

explanation.surface: Asking why Celtic peoples are making such a racket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hue and cry' looks like one idiom; 'hue' is the definition and 'cry' begins the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A yellowish-brown earth colour.

clue.text: Had a row in the ring with an extremist

parts.note: a ring is round, the shape of the letter O
a red is a revolutionary left-winger, an extremist

explanation.surface: A boxer brawling in the ring with a radical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Had a row' looks like a quarrel; it is rowing a boat, so the verb means used oars.
explanation.definitionFit: Propelled a boat with oars, which is rowing.

definitions.meaning: Caleb ... is the honest land agent in George Eliot's novel Middlemarch
an old northern word for an enclosed yard or garden

explanation.surface: A man named Caleb from Scotland Yard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the Yard' suggests Scotland Yard detectives, but it is just an enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: Caleb is Eliot's land agent in Middlemarch, and the word also means an enclosed courtyard or garden.

clue.text: Move around to the depot in a measure of mechanized transport

parts.note: to wheel is to turn or move round in a circle
a base is a depot from which operations are run

explanation.surface: Driving round to a depot with some form of vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: The distance between a vehicle's front and rear axles is a measure belonging to motor transport.
explanation.definitionFit: The distance between front and rear axles, a standard measurement of a car or lorry.

parts.note: Keats's simile for a pale face, primroses being pale and picked in darkness

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank from Keats's Endymion: the missing word is the pallor of primroses picked at night.
explanation.definitionFit: Pale and sickly-looking, like flowers seen at night.

parts.note: in A Midsummer Night's Dream Starveling plays Moonshine and carries a light as his stage prop

explanation.surface: An attribute of illicit liquor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Property' is a theatrical prop: Moonshine, in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream, carries a lamp, a thornbush and a dog. 'Moonshine' looks like illicit spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: A portable lamp in a protective case, the prop carried by the actor playing the moon.

clue.text: A coat to cover the wide boy?

definitions.text: A coat to cover the wide boy?

parts.words: A coat to cover the wide boy?
parts.note: a long overcoat whose French name means over everything, as if wide enough to cover all

explanation.surface: A coat for a flashy spiv.
explanation.walkthrough: The French name means 'over all', a garment worn over everything else; 'wide boy' is British slang for a shady dealer, here a stout figure needing wide cover.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's long close-fitting overcoat of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries.
